one_liner: Plugin-based C media framework; its VA-API pipelines decoded and encoded on an Intel iGPU 1.2-10x faster than OpenCV's software FFmpeg backend.
what_it_does: GStreamer builds media pipelines from elements (sources, demuxers, decoders, converters, encoders, muxers, sinks) linked by caps negotiation and run in their own streaming threads. Codecs come from plugins: gst-libav wraps libavcodec, and the VA-API elements (the measured gstreamer-vaapi vaapidecodebin/vaapih264enc, now replaced by the va plugin's vah264dec/vah264enc in gst-plugins-bad) drive the GPU's fixed-function codecs. In the benchmark it is reached through OpenCV: VideoCapture/VideoWriter with CAP_GSTREAMER and a gst-launch style pipeline string ending in appsink or starting with appsrc, instead of CAP_FFMPEG with a file name.
how_it_is_fast: The headline wins are hardware offload, not faster software: vaapidecodebin and vaapih264enc/vaapivp8enc hand the bitstream to the Skylake GT2 media engine through libva, so the CPU only demuxes, copies surfaces back and colour-converts. The pipeline also overlaps work across threads (demuxer, decoder queue, converter and the application run concurrently), and in the OpenCV sample the GStreamer pipelines convert colour with videoconvert n-threads set to OpenCV's thread count, while the FFmpeg backend converts with a single sws_scale call (SWS_BICUBIC) on the calling thread.
when_to_use: Linux machines with an Intel or AMD GPU and a working VA-API driver that must encode H.264, HEVC or VP8 faster than software encoders can, e.g. writing many 720p/1080p streams from an OpenCV or camera application where the measured gap was 3.7-3.8x for H.264 and about 10x for VP8.
Decoding H.264/HEVC from MP4 or AVI on such hardware while freeing CPU cores: the page measured 376 vs 169 fps (mp4/h264) and 391 vs 256 fps (mp4/h265) at 1080p to BGR.
Applications that need a full pipeline (capture, RTSP/WebRTC, muxing, compositing) with swappable hardware backends (VA, NVCODEC, V4L2, MediaSDK/QSV) rather than a single codec library.
OpenCV programs on Linux that already have WITH_GSTREAMER builds and can express their I/O as a pipeline string.
when_not_to_use: Matroska input on the measured stack: gst-vaapi decoded every mkv clip far slower than FFmpeg (h264 59 vs 158, h265 65 vs 255, vp8 68 vs 309 fps); the page gives no explanation, so test your container before switching.
Pure CPU decoding: gst-libav wraps the same libavcodec and lost to OpenCV's FFmpeg backend on h264, h265 and vp8 decode and on mpeg2 encode (81 vs 106 fps).

When compression efficiency or quality per bit matters: hardware encoders at VA-API defaults were compared with libx264 CRF 23 and libvpx good-quality output, with no bitrate or quality figures, so the speed buys an unmeasured quality loss.
Machines without a supported GPU and VA driver (or non-Linux targets for the VA elements); the speedup does not exist there.

As evidence against FFmpeg itself: FFmpeg's own VA-API path was never measured, and current OpenCV 4.x can enable VA-API in its FFmpeg backend (cap_ffmpeg_hw.hpp, VIDEO_ACCELERATION_VAAPI), removing the 2018 reason for the comparison.

integration.form: shared lib (libgstreamer-1.0 core plus dynamically loaded plugin libraries)
integration.dependencies: GLib/GObject, libintl, zlib, libffi (mandatory, bundled as meson subprojects); for this result libva plus a VA driver and the VA plugin, gst-libav needs FFmpeg; OpenCV built with -DWITH_GSTREAMER=ON to use it from OpenCV
integration.min_toolchain: C compiler; building the monorepo needs Meson 1.4+, ninja and Python 3.8+ (README); measured with Ubuntu 17.10 packages (GStreamer 1.12 series)
integration.platforms: Linux, Windows, macOS, Android, iOS for the core; VA-API elements are Linux-oriented and need Intel/AMD hardware decode/encode support for the codec
integration.thread_safety: Pipelines run on internal streaming threads; the thread-safety contract of the API was not read this session (not documented in the sources read)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — in OpenCV you swap CAP_FFMPEG for CAP_GSTREAMER and pass a pipeline string (e.g. filesrc ! qtdemux ! vaapidecodebin ! videoconvert ! appsink); outside OpenCV it is a different framework API from libavcodec/libavformat

gotchas: Harness asymmetry in the OpenCV 3.4 sample and backends: GStreamer pipelines colour-convert with videoconvert n-threads=getNumThreads() (4 on the i5-6600) while the FFmpeg backend converts each 1080p frame to BGR24 with one single-threaded sws_scale inside the timed retrieve; and OpenCV's FFmpeg writer never sets thread_count, so libvpx (VP8, deadline good, cpu-used 1) and FFmpeg's mpeg2video encoder ran single-threaded (libx264 alone gets automatic threads from its codec defaults). The 10.3x VP8 and 1.2x MPEG-2 encode ratios are therefore hardware versus one CPU core, and part of the CPU-side gaps (including gst-libav's mpeg2 decode wins) is conversion threading, not codec speed.

Encode timing covers only the VideoWriter write call: GStreamer's appsrc (block=1, default max-bytes) returns once the previous frame is dequeued, so encoding overlaps the untimed synthetic-frame grab; FFmpeg's x264 lookahead frames and GStreamer's in-flight frames are flushed in close(), also untimed. The input is 1000 identical videotestsrc SMPTE colour-bar frames (default 720p, 30 fps target), not real video, and the output files are never decoded or checked.

The measured plugin is gone: gstreamer-vaapi was removed from the monorepo on 2025-06-10 ('gstreamer-vaapi: remove subproject', after 1.26.0); current code uses the va plugin in gst-plugins-bad (vah264enc since 1.22, plus vah265, vavp8, vavp9, av1 and jpeg elements), which this benchmark never measured. The OpenCV sample still names vaapi elements.

Licensing: the core is LGPL-2.1-or-later, but some plugins with GPL dependencies (x265enc, mpeg2enc, the sample's 'gst-basic' MPEG-2 encoder) are only built with -Dgpl=enabled. Container parsers have had many CVEs (e.g. the December 2024 batch for matroskademux and qtdemux fixed in 1.24.10), so keep it updated when handling untrusted files.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick GStreamer when you need GPU-offloaded encode or decode inside a full streaming pipeline on Linux; for decoding straight into arrays from Python, Nelux (FFmpeg with NVDEC) or video_reader-rs (beats OpenCV VideoCapture) are simpler, and for a faster pure-software H.264 decoder edge264 or rivet-h26x target libavcodec directly.
verified_claims_summary: OpenCV's 2018 wiki benchmark (single runs, Ubuntu 17.10 packages, Core i5-6600 with HD Graphics 530) timed its gstreamer_pipeline sample: gst-vaapi encoded 1000 synthetic frames at 193/194/185 fps H.264 and 124 fps VP8 versus 51/51/50 and 12 fps through OpenCV's FFmpeg writer, and decoded 1080p mp4/avi H.264 at 376/373 fps versus 169/159 fps, but lost on every mkv input. It is iGPU fixed-function hardware against CPU software codecs with unequal conversion threading and encoder settings, not GStreamer's own code against FFmpeg's.
status_note: Actively developed (GitHub read-only mirror of gitlab.freedesktop.org, 126k commits, last commit 2026-10-11) and LGPL-2.1-or-later, so linking is usable in closed products; the measured gstreamer-vaapi plugin was removed in June 2025 in favour of the va plugin, so the numbers describe a component you can no longer get from main.
